prime.problem: "Which layout?" has no answer until you know how many users must be held at once, at what context and speed. Size by weights alone and a 70B model "fits on one H100" with room for two chats; size by total tokens per second and you miss memory and failures entirely.
prime.fits: Last card of the course, the capstone. It reuses the pipeline card's step-time model and layout throughputs, expert parallelism's big units, and DeepSeek-V3's deployment sizes, and adds memory budgets, traffic, failure and dollars.
expect: VRAM math: n·u·M ≥ W + A + U·c·b_kv
minimum GPUs per model, precision and GPU type
users held at once set the replica count; TPOT rarely binds for chat
prime.goal: Size a deployment for a given model, precision, GPU, user count, context and speed target in four passes (memory, traffic, layout, failure) and price it.

attend: Why is "the weights fit" never the answer to how many GPUs you need?
In the 500-user example, which constraint sets the GPU count, memory or the 50 ms TPOT?
Why does TP4 × 4 survive a GPU failure so much better than TP8 × 2 on the same 16 GPUs?
Why is the H200 cheaper per token here despite a higher hourly price?
When is "smallest TP × many replicas" the wrong answer?

must: Every resident user's KV must fit next to the weights in the usable memory (u = 0.92) → KV room = n·u·M − W decides users per replica → users held at once ÷ users per replica = replicas → for chat, memory (not speed) sets the GPU count: 500 users of 70B FP8 at 4k need 16 H100s or 8 H200s

Each replica's step must stay under the per-user TPOT → bigger batches make steps slower → the batch is min(what fits, what meets the TPOT) → at 20 tok/s every layout has room; at 40 tok/s TP8's batch must drop from 386 to 333 → speed targets start deciding the layout around there

A TP or EP group runs in lockstep → one dead GPU stops the whole group → group MTBF ≈ 50,000 GPU-hours ÷ group size (TP4 ≈ 521 days, EP320 ≈ 6.5 days) → smaller replicas lose less capacity per failure (TP4 × 4 keeps 99.6%, TP8 × 2 77%) and make an N+1 spare cheaper

$ per token = $/hour ÷ tokens per hour → when memory binds, a GPU with more HBM holds more users per dollar → 8 H200s at $4.59/GPU-hr ≈ $1.02 per million vs 16 H100s at $1.77 → price the constraint, not the peak FLOPs
elevated: Kiely's headroom rule (KV room ≥ ½ W) and his note that KV often takes 80%+ of post-weight VRAM → a model that barely fits serves almost no one → minimum-fit tables are lower bounds, pass 2 is the real count
reference: vLLM's gpu_memory_utilization default (0.92, older 0.9) and max_num_batched_tokens
Lambda and RunPod prices on the fetch date

compress.prompt: From memory, write the four passes as a numbered list with one arrow chain each (memory → users per replica, traffic → replicas, layout → TP/PP/EP, failure → spare). Then write the VRAM inequality and the $/M-token formula.
checklist: n·u·M ≥ W + activations + users × context × KV bytes per token
replicas = users held at once ÷ users per replica, checked against the TPOT
TP inside a node for speed, replicas for capacity, PP/EP only when one copy must span nodes
group MTBF ≈ 50,000 h ÷ GPUs; add one spare replica

retrieve.q: Explain why "users held at once" rather than "total tokens per second" sets the GPU count for a chat service, with the card's 500 vs 250-user example.
answer: each resident user needs their KV in GPU memory for the whole conversation
10,000 tok/s is both 500 users × 20 tok/s and 250 × 40 tok/s
the first needs KV for 500 users (16 H100s), the second for 250 (8 H100s as TP4 × 2), even at the same throughput

retrieve.q: Walk through pass 1 and pass 2 for one TP4 replica of Llama-3.1-70B in FP8 on H100s at 4k context: KV pool, users per replica, step time, and replica count for 500 users.
answer: pool = 4 × 0.92 × 80 − 70.6 = 223.8 GB; 4k context = 1.342 GB per user → 166 users

retrieve.q: Your team must choose between TP8 × 2 and TP4 × 4 on 16 H100s for the 500-user workload. Compare them on latency, failure and the cost of an N+1 spare, and choose.
answer: both pass the 50 ms TPOT at full load (TP8 28.1 ms with 386 users per replica, TP4 24.3 ms with 166); at batch 1 TP8 is faster (7.62 vs 11.70 ms)
one GPU failure: TP4 × 4 keeps 498 users (99.6%), TP8 × 2 keeps 386 (77%)
N+1 costs 4 GPUs for TP4, 8 for TP8 ($79.80 vs $95.76 per hour)
choose TP4 × 4 unless per-user speed is the product

compare.q: The pipeline card ranked layouts by throughput at 8k with every sequence packed in; this card sizes for a user count. Why can the two answers differ, and which question does each answer?
answer: the pipeline card asks how many tokens a fixed set of GPUs can produce (a ceiling)
this card asks how few GPUs hold a given set of users at a TPOT target
at 8k one TP8 weight copy leaves the most KV room, so it wins throughput; for 500 users at 4k, TP4 × 4 uses the same 16 GPUs and fails more gracefully

compare.q: DeepSeek's 144-GPU decode unit vs this card's small-replica advice: what does each optimise, and what is the failure cost of each?
answer: DeepSeek optimises per-expert batch size, so it needs a big EP group
this card optimises memory per user and graceful degradation for a dense model
EP144's group MTBF is ≈ 347 h (≈ 14.5 days) and a failure takes 18 nodes out; a TP4 replica's is ≈ 521 days and costs half a node
huge MoEs at high volume accept the exposure; dense models usually shouldn't

predict.q: Change the pass-2 workload to 300 users at 8k context (70B FP8, H100 TP4, 20 tok/s). How many replicas and GPUs, including one spare, and does the TPOT bind? Commit first.
predict.answer: An 8k user needs 2.68 GB of KV, so a 223.8 GB pool holds 83 users; ⌈300 ÷ 83⌉ = 4 replicas = 16 H100s, 20 with a spare. The step at 83 users is ≈ (17.64 + 83 × 2.68 ÷ 4) ÷ 3.35 ≈ 21.9 ms + ≈ 1.7 ms of all-reduces ≈ 23.6 ms, well under 50 ms: memory still binds. Doubling context halved users per replica, so it took the same GPUs as 500 users at 4k.

apply.task: Run python3 labs/sizing.py --model llama-70b --prec fp8 --gpu h100 --users 300 --tok-s 20 --ctx 8192 and check it against your hand answer to the predict question. Then run the same with --gpu h200 and compare two layouts by hand: H200 TP1 (usable 0.92 × 141 GB) and H200 TP2. For each give users per replica, replicas, GPUs, and the MTBF of one replica.
apply.done: The lab's H100 answer matches your hand calculation, and you have users per replica, replica count, GPU count and replica MTBF for both H200 layouts.
apply.hint: H200 TP1: 0.92 × 141 − 70.6 = 59.1 GB → 22 users of 2.68 GB → ⌈300/22⌉ = 14 replicas = 14 GPUs, MTBF 50,000 h ≈ 5.7 years each. H200 TP2: 2 × 129.7 − 70.6 = 188.8 GB → 70 users → 5 replicas = 10 GPUs, MTBF 25,000 h ≈ 1,042 days. TP2 needs fewer GPUs because it holds one weight copy per 2 GPUs.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: that 300 users at 8k need the same GPUs as 500 at 4k?
Could you explain why memory, not speed, usually sets the count for chat?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: context → KV per user → users per replica, or group size → MTBF?
Would you now trust a vendor's "fits on N GPUs" claim? What would you ask first?
Which number here would you most want the rented-node script to measure, and why?
